title: TAKE IT DOWN Act (Public Law 119-12, 139 Stat. 55)

covered_actors: Any person in interstate or foreign commerce using an interactive computer service to knowingly publish or threaten to publish nonconsensual authentic intimate visual depictions or AI-generated digital forgeries

Covered platforms (public websites, online services, online applications, and mobile applications primarily providing user-generated content forums or regularly hosting/curating nonconsensual intimate visual depictions, including nonprofits)
prohibited_practices: Knowingly publishing via an interactive computer service in interstate or foreign commerce an authentic nonconsensual intimate visual depiction of an identifiable adult (subject to privacy, non-public-concern, and harm elements) or of a minor with intent to abuse, humiliate, harass, degrade, or arouse/gratify sexual desire

Knowingly publishing via an interactive computer service in interstate or foreign commerce an AI-generated or technologically created digital forgery intimate visual depiction of an identifiable adult without consent or of a minor with prohibited intent
Intentionally threatening to publish a nonconsensual authentic intimate visual depiction or digital forgery for intimidation, coercion, extortion, or to create mental distress

enforcement_authorities: U.S. Department of Justice / federal prosecutors and federal courts (criminal offenses, forfeiture, and restitution under 47 U.S.C. 223(h) and Title 18)
compliance_deadlines: 2025-05-19: Enactment and immediate effectiveness of Section 2 criminal prohibitions amending 47 U.S.C. 223(h)
2026-05-19 (not later than 1 year after May 19, 2025 enactment): Covered platforms must establish the written notice-and-removal process and publish plain-language notice

Within 48 hours of receiving a valid removal request: Covered platforms must remove the nonconsensual intimate visual depiction and make reasonable efforts to identify and remove known identical copies
policy_extraction.penalties_summary: Criminal penalties under 47 U.S.C. 223(h) include Title 18 fines and up to 2 years imprisonment (adults) or 3 years (minors) for unlawful publication of authentic depictions or AI digital forgeries; threats involving digital forgeries carry Title 18 fines and up to 18 months (adults) or 30 months (minors) imprisonment (threats involving authentic depictions carry the 2-year/3-year maximums), plus mandatory criminal forfeiture of illicit materials, proceeds, and facilitating property and mandatory restitution under 18 U.S.C. 2264. Platform failure to reasonably comply with Section 3 notice-and-takedown duties is treated as an FTC Section 18(a)(1)(B) UDAP rule violation subject to full FTC Act civil penalties and enforcement powers, explicitly extending to nonprofits.
policy_extraction.implementation_notes: Public Law 119-12 (139 Stat. 55), approved May 19, 2025. First binding U.S. federal statute targeting AI-generated nonconsensual intimate visual depictions ('digital forgeries') alongside authentic NCII. Section 2 amends Section 223 of the Communications Act of 1934 to create federal criminal offenses; Section 3 mandates a covered-platform notice-and-takedown regime within 1 year (by May 19, 2026) requiring 48-hour removal and reasonable efforts to remove known identical copies, backed by good-faith takedown liability immunity and FTC UDAP rule-violation enforcement. Excludes broadband ISPs, email, and primarily non-UGC preselected-content services.

risk_framing.rationale_summary: The TAKE IT DOWN Act is dominantly framed around consumer_public_safety, targeting exploitation, abuse, harassment, extortion, and concrete psychological, financial, and reputational harm to individuals—with heightened protection for minors—through federal criminalization and FTC unfair-and-deceptive-practices platform takedown enforcement. Consumer_public_safety edges out fundamental_rights because the statute anchors liability in tangible victim harm, child protection, anti-extortion, and consumer-protection UDAP enforcement rather than constitutional-rights declarations. Fundamental_rights is a strong secondary frame grounded in affirmative voluntary consent, reasonable expectations of personal privacy, and free-expression carve-outs for matters of public concern.
